html:
Ptolemaic Egypt was a Greek kingdom in Egypt founded by Ptolemy I, a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great, and ruled by his descendants from 305 BCE until the death of Cleopatra VII in 30 BCE. It was the longest-lasting of the kingdoms carved out of Alexander's empire.

Ptolemy took Egypt soon after Alexander died in 323 BCE, and even seized Alexander's body for burial in his capital, Alexandria. The Ptolemies made Alexandria the leading city of the Greek world:

  • The Library of Alexandria tried to collect every book in Greek, and scholars there measured the earth, edited Homer and translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.
  • The Lighthouse on the island of Pharos was one of the Seven Wonders.

The kings ruled two peoples at once. To Greeks they were Macedonian kings; to Egyptians they were pharaohs, and they built great temples to the old gods at Edfu, Dendera and Philae. Decrees were written in Greek and Egyptian, as on the Rosetta Stone of 196 BCE. Greeks held most high posts, and the royal family spoke Greek; Cleopatra VII was said to be the first of them to learn Egyptian. Kings often married their own sisters, following pharaoh custom.

The Ptolemies fought six wars with the Seleucids over Syria. From the second century BCE they grew weaker and leaned on Rome. Cleopatra allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony. After their defeat at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, Rome took Egypt in 30 BCE, and its grain began to feed Rome.
